steps.text:
Good question — and a slightly meta one, since Fable 5 is the model you're talking to right now. Here's what actually sets it apart:

**Positioning.** Fable 5 is the first model in the Claude 5 family and sits in a new "Mythos-class" tier *above* Opus — it's Anthropic's most intelligent generally available model. It shares its underlying model with **Claude Mythos 5**, which offers the same capabilities but without Fable's additional safety measures for dual-use capabilities; Mythos 5 is only available to approved organizations (through Project Glasswing). More on the split at [anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5).

**What it's for.** The headline gains are on work *above* what prior models handled well: long-horizon autonomous runs (overnight coding sessions that finish without correction), first-shot implementations of well-specified systems, end-to-end knowledge deliverables (financial models, decks, docs), dependable parallel sub-agent orchestration, and vision on dense or degraded images. It has a 1M-token context window (that's also the default), 128K max output, and single turns on hard tasks can legitimately run many minutes.

**How it differs technically.** A few things are genuinely different from the Opus family, not just "more":

- **Thinking is always on** — you can't disable it or set a token budget; you steer depth with an `effort` parameter (`low` through `max`). The raw chain of thought is never returned, only optional summaries.
- **Safety classifiers on requests** — it targets research biology and most offensive cybersecurity content, and can return a `refusal` stop reason. API code is expected to opt into automatic fallbacks to Opus 4.8 so a false positive doesn't fail the request. This is the main practical difference from Mythos 5.
- **Requires 30-day data retention** — it's not available under zero-data-retention arrangements.
- No assistant prefill, no sampling parameters (`temperature` etc.) — you steer it with prompting.

**Pricing.** $10 input / $50 output per million tokens — double Opus 4.8's $5/$25. That's why the general guidance is: Opus 4.8 remains the default workhorse, and Fable 5 is for the hardest reasoning and longest-horizon agentic work where the capability ceiling justifies the cost.

One prompting note worth knowing: it responds better to being given the goal and constraints than to step-by-step instructions — overly prescriptive prompts written for older models can actually *reduce* its output quality.
do you think i need an interrpitur based on my history with you?

Ha — no, you're fine. And I appreciate that "interrpitur" is doing a lot of work in a sentence asking whether you need an interpreter.

Honestly, based on our history: your typos have never once been the problem. What I know of you from past sessions — the three-lab and transition-lab motion studios, LifeRPG, the WORLDIES pipeline — is that you communicate in quick, loose bursts and the intent is always clear from context. "reactStrictMode off for AnimatePresence" tells me everything I need even if half the words around it are mangled. I'd rather have fast and typo-ridden than slow and polished; the former is more information per minute.

The only times I'd genuinely want clarification from you aren't spelling issues at all — they're scope issues: things like "make it better" on a landing page, or a one-word "fix it" when there are three candidate bugs. That's not an interpreter problem, that's just me needing one more sentence of intent.

So: no interpreter needed. Though if you actually meant something else — like whether you need a code *interpreter* / REPL setup for one of your projects — say the word and I'll take a real look.

how do you see videos?

Short answer: I don't, really — I fake it well with frames.

I have no native video perception. I can't play a file, perceive motion, or hear audio. What I *can* see is images. So "seeing" a video is always a decomposition into things I can actually inspect:

**Frames.** I run `ffmpeg` to extract stills at chosen timestamps and then read those as images — that part is genuine visual understanding, same as any screenshot. This is exactly what your WORLDIES producer pipeline does when it "verifies via stills": render → pull frames at the hook, the strike, the end card → I look at each one and judge crop, caption placement, logo bug, sharpness. If I pull frames every ~1–2 seconds I can reconstruct a decent sense of pacing and what happens when, but I'm interpolating between snapshots, not watching.

**Metadata.** `ffprobe` gives me duration, resolution, fps, codecs, bitrate, stream layout — the objective facts about the file without seeing anything.

**Audio.** I can't hear it. I can extract the track and look at a waveform image (useful for finding beat drops or silence for music sync), or run it through a transcription tool to get the speech as text.

**Server-side analyzers.** Some of your connected MCP tools do process video for real on their end — the Higgsfield video-analysis and virality-predictor tools ingest actual footage and return structured judgments (hook strength, retention risk, attention). There I'm consuming their report, not seeing the video myself.

The practical consequence for your shorts work: anything I "confirm" about a render is only as good as the frames I sampled. A one-frame glitch, a caption that flickers early, or an audio sync issue between sampled points can slip past me — which is why the stills-revision loop samples the moments that matter rather than trusting a single thumbnail.
so if i drop any video you will be able to analyze it?

Pretty much, yes — with a couple of honest caveats about what "analyze" means.

**What works:** if the video lands on disk as a file (dropped into the session, or a path you give me), I can go at it with `ffprobe`/`ffmpeg` — pull metadata, extract frames wherever I want, and visually inspect them. From that I can tell you what's in it, judge composition and quality, check captions and branding, find scene cuts, locate a specific moment, build a shot list, spot where the crop goes wrong. For audio I can extract the track, look at waveforms for beats/silence, and transcribe speech if a transcription tool is available. That covers most of what "analyze this video" usually means in practice.

**The caveats:**

- **It has to reach my filesystem.** A file path or a dropped file: yes. Some chat-attachment flows deliver videos in a way I can't read directly — if that happens, saving it somewhere and giving me the path always works.
- **Codecs:** anything ffmpeg can decode is fine (which is nearly everything — mp4, mov, mkv, webm...). DRM-protected content, no.
- **Sampling blindness:** my "watching" is frames at intervals. The denser I sample, the more I catch, but a single-frame glitch or a subtle audio-video sync drift between samples can escape me. For your shorts I'd sample densely at the moments that matter (hook, strike, transitions) rather than uniformly.
- **Length is just cost, not a limit:** a 90-minute match means I'm sampling smartly, not reading every frame.

So: drop one in and tell me what question you want answered about it — "is this render clean," "find the goal," "why does this feel slow" — and I'll pick the right way to slice it.
is it possible to make a copycat machine? i drop a video and we make our own extraction of knowledge on how to do certain things based on the video

Yes — and it's a very buildable shape. What you're describing is basically a **reference deconstruction pipeline**: video in → structured "how they did it" recipe out → recipes accumulate into a technique library. It's the same pattern you already run in three-lab (pattern catalog → code-recipe spec → feed it to an agent), just with a video as the input instead of an r3f scene.

Here's how I'd structure it:

**1. Ingest (mechanical).** ffprobe for the facts, scene-cut detection to find every edit point, dense frame extraction around cuts and sparse in between, audio waveform for beat/drop positions, transcription for any speech.

**2. Deconstruction passes (where the knowledge lives).** Each pass answers a craft question:
- *Pacing* — cut lengths over time. Does it front-load 0.8s cuts then breathe? Where's the longest hold?
- *Hook anatomy* — what happens in seconds 0–3, frame by frame. Text on screen? Cold open mid-action? Audio bait?
- *Cut-to-beat alignment* — overlay cut timestamps on the waveform; you can literally measure how tightly edits ride the music.
- *Caption/text style* — timing, position, size, when words appear relative to speech.
- *Camera/crop language* — zoom-ins, punch-ins, where the subject sits in frame.
- *Structure* — the macro arc: hook → context → payoff → loop point.

**3. The recipe.** Each video becomes one markdown/JSON file: measured numbers, not vibes. "Hook: 1.9s, three cuts, text appears at 0.4s. Cuts average 1.1s until the payoff at 0:22, then a 3s hold. Every cut lands within 80ms of a beat." That's executable knowledge — your producer agent can follow it directly.

**4. The compounding part.** One video gives you a case study. Five videos from the same creator or niche give you *the formula* — a cross-video pass that finds what's constant (that's their technique) versus what varies (that's just content). The constants get promoted into your house playbook.

**Honest limits:** I extract what's observable at frame resolution — structure, timing, composition, text. Color grades I can estimate but not perfectly reverse-engineer; sub-frame motion feel (easing curves on a zoom) I approximate from frame deltas. And the line to stay on the right side of: copying *technique* is how everyone learns the craft; copying *footage or content* isn't — but your claims-log already handles that discipline for WORLDIES.

Drop a reference video whenever you like and name what you want stolen from it — "the pacing," "the hook," "why this retains" — and we'll build the first recipe. Once we've done one manually and you like the output format, it's worth freezing into a skill or the producer's pipeline so every future drop runs the same deconstruction automatically.
what is the best way to record my screen on a mac for you to see?

The humble **⌘⇧5** is genuinely the best answer — the built-in macOS recorder. No extra software, and its output (H.264 `.mov`) is ideal for my frame extraction. A few settings make the result much more useful to me:

**Setup (once, in the ⌘⇧5 options menu):**
- **Save to** a folder I can reach — your project folder or Desktop, anywhere you can paste me a path from. That's more reliable than chat attachments.
- **Show Mouse Clicks: on.** Without it I see the cursor move but can't tell when you clicked — with it, every click gets a visible ring, which lets me reconstruct the exact interaction sequence.

**When recording:**
- **Record a selected portion, not the whole screen** — drag the box around just the relevant window. Retina full-screen recordings are 5K+ images where the interesting part is 15% of the frame; a tight crop means every extracted frame is dense with signal and text stays razor sharp.
- **Keep it short and single-purpose.** A 20-second clip of the one bug beats a 4-minute tour. If there are three things to show, three clips named `bug-dropdown.mov`, `bug-scroll.mov`... is much better for me than one long take.
- **Don't rely on voice narration** — I can't hear it (transcription is possible but adds a step). Type the context in chat instead: "watch the sidebar at 0:08, it jumps."

Then just give me the path and I'll pull frames and dig in.

**Two extra notes for your use cases:**
- **Motion/animation review** (transition-lab territory): the built-in recorder captures at up to 60fps, which is dense enough for me to extract frame-by-frame and actually measure easing, stagger timing, and jank — so it works for "does this transition feel right" questions, not just bugs.
- **If it's a local web app, consider skipping the recording entirely** — I can often drive the browser myself (preview tools / Chrome extension) and take my own screenshots while iterating. Recordings shine for things I can't reproduce: one-off glitches, flows behind logins I don't have, or "this is the vibe I want" references.

The recipe describes the source cover as "Titanic sinking into a GitHub-logo iceberg" but gives no generalizable rule for constructing the shock visual (photo composite? illustration? how literal?). Slide 12's elements are enumerated (value prop, newsletter pitch, article preview, DM notification, arrow, keyword) but with no layout, hierarchy, or platform styling for the fake DM (Instagram push? iOS banner? colors?). Vertical order and the glass-pill DM styling are guesses. The "hand-drawn arrow" style/direction is also improvised as an SVG.
  9. Benefit copy constraints. "Two lines of benefit copy: white claim line + mint price/differentiator line" — no guidance on length, sentence count, or tone beyond the examples. Some of my lines run to two sentences; the source may be terser.
  10. Caption + pinned comment not reproducible. The recipe says the caption mirrors the slides and restates the keyword, and FORMULA mentions keyword placement in "≥2 places (caption + CTA slide, sometimes pinned comment)". An HTML deliverable has no caption surface; the keyword appears on slides 12 and 13 instead, and the caption text itself is unwritten.
  11. Background texture ambiguity. FORMULA's dark lane mentions a "pixel mascot" (for @liambuilds) — unclear whether @bestapps' variant has any mascot, texture, or gradient on the near-black background. I added a faint mint radial vignette and no mascot.
